prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B045 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case rests on the science and not on the unanimous opening. Holst established human incretin physiology, Drucker worked out GLP-1 and GLP-2 receptor biology and mechanism, and Mojsov is credited with the active truncated GLP-1(7-36) form. Together they define the physiology that long-acting agonists then exploited, and large independent outcome trials confirm the effects on glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The achievement is mature, mechanistically clear and opened a new area of gut-pancreas-brain signalling, so it is a discovery prize and not a drug-development award. I considered the two-part idea I raised in round 1 (B045 reduced to two names plus B015). I now reject it. It would drop one of the three people who each hold a distinct, identifiable part of the discovery chain, and nothing in round 1 argues that the GLP-1 case is strong enough to survive that cut without harm.
statement.case_against: The weak point is still attribution. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide form is contested, and Habener is outside the credited names. Nothing in the materials I am allowed to read lets me resolve that priority, and I have not checked primary literature, so I cannot say her claim is secure. Leaving out Knudsen also has a cost: a prize that stops at physiology can be read as passing over the person who engineered the acylated analogues that made once-daily and once-weekly drugs possible. The commercial scale of semaglutide and tirzepatide may also make the underlying discovery look larger or smaller than it is. I accept these risks because the alternative configurations carry attribution problems of their own that are not smaller.

responses.point: Sten agreed that the Mojsov-Habener balance is the main risk, and said the committee should check the primary literature on the active truncated peptide before the final ballot, and that he would revisit the trio if her claim proved weaker than assumed.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and I will not claim more than I know. The materials available at this stage do not contain a primary-source record, so I cannot check who first identified and synthesised the active peptide, and I will not treat her priority as settled. What I can say is that the other members, myself included, rest the third seat on Mojsov's identification of the active form, and the argument that a priority dispute does not erase a real contribution is a fair one. If a primary-source check were to show her claim to be materially weaker, I would move to Knudsen in her place and would say so openly, since that keeps the prize with credited names on the list and puts the drug design inside the award. I would not drop the single-part structure for it.

responses.point: Abdel opened with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the long-acting analogue design is a real mechanistic contribution, and later moved to the Mojsov trio while still saying that excluding Knudsen has a cost and that I discount optogenetics as a research tool.
responses.response: I agree that Knudsen's acylation strategy was a real mechanistic idea. Turning a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a weekly drug was not routine formulation. I am keeping Mojsov mainly because the identification of the active peptide is upstream of everything the pharmacology used, and the citation can name the therapeutic outcome without crediting the engineering. On optogenetics, you are right that I should state my position more precisely. I do not discount it for being a tool. A method that enables causal, cell-type-specific tests is a discovery in physiology. What keeps B006 below the cleaner candidates for me is the six-name credit problem: my own round-1 trio (Deisseroth, Boyden, Miesenböck) differs from yours (Deisseroth, Nagel, Hegemann), and we cannot both be right. That is a credit problem, not a judgement about clinical impact.

responses.point: Per rates the UPR attribution as clean but hesitates over its weaker disease link next to HPV, and sees B015 as a strong alternative and not the preferred prize this year. He also asks whether the committee wants mechanism or demonstrated patient benefit.
responses.response: I accept the reservation and have acted on it. I rated B015 second in the opening because Walter and Mori have a conceptually original, clean two-person credit. But the committee's own round-1 record shows that neither Per nor Thomas would put it ahead of GLP-1, and I do not see a reason to create a two-part prize that cuts GLP-1 to two names. Your point that the disease link of the UPR is still developing is a fair counterweight to my mechanism-first view. I would not push for B015 this year, and I would put it as a strong later candidate. I keep it as an alternative because it is the best-attributed ballot on the shortlist.

responses.point: Thomas rates B003 as a mature case of basic virology giving cancer prevention, and would change his mind about the third B045 seat only if the citation is meant to cover the drugs, in which case Knudsen would replace Mojsov and the choice should be stated openly.
responses.response: I agree that the choice should be explicit, and I think this is the right way to put it. The trio with Mojsov is a statement that the prize is for physiology and identification of the active peptide, and the citation says so. A Knudsen version would be a statement about the drugs. I prefer the first because it is closer to what we usually reward and because five of the six members independently arrived at it. On B003, I still hold it as a first alternative but my view of its priority record has not changed. Lowy, Schiller and Frazer are a defensible trio, but Zhou cannot be recognised, parallel VLP groups exist, and I cannot resolve Frazer's priority from what I may read. That is why it remains an alternative and not my preferred prize.

responses.point: Marie ranked B003 second and said a one-achievement prize with the three GLP-1 names is cleaner than any split configuration, while raising long-term safety and durability as open questions.
responses.response: I agree that a single-part prize is cleaner, and that is what moved me off the two-part option. On long-term safety I would say the open durability questions do not weaken the discovery claim, because the physiology and the mechanism are already confirmed independently. They bear on how the drugs are used, which is a matter for clinicians and not for the award. I would not word the citation in a way that promises long-term outcomes.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide over Habener is secure. I cannot verify it from the permitted materials, and a primary-source check could change the third name to Knudsen.
Whether the committee wants the citation to cover physiology and the active peptide only, or the translation into acylated long-acting drugs as well.
How much the Zhou issue, parallel VLP groups and the 2008 zur Hausen prize should weigh against B003 if GLP-1 attribution fails.
Whether UPR disease relevance, which is still developing, is a lasting limit on B015 or a matter of timing.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén, and neither is credited on any shortlisted ballot, nor connected to any shortlisted candidate, so I see no recusal need. My own work on single-cell methods and transcription does not involve any credited name on B045, B003 or B015. I did not rely on any private information about the committee or votes.
